01
Networking · from the subnetting guide

Subnet calculator

Enter any IPv4 address and move the CIDR slider to see the network split in real time.

/24

Reading it: the network address names the subnet itself and the broadcast address talks to everyone in it — neither can be given to a device, which is why a /24 has 254 usable hosts, not 256.

← All tools
02
Cyber safety · from the passwords guide

Password strength checker

Type a password you are thinking of using and see how long it would actually hold up.

Start typing…
  • 12+ characters
  • Lowercase letters
  • Uppercase letters
  • Numbers
  • Symbols
  • Not a common password

Estimates assume an offline attack on a leaked fast hash at ~10 billion guesses per second. Length beats clever symbols every time — four random words outperform most “complex” 8-character passwords.

04
Networking · from the IP addresses guide

IP inspector

Paste any IP address to validate it and see what class it is, whether it is private, and how it looks in binary.

Quick test: try 127.0.0.1 (loopback — your own machine), 169.254.1.5 (link-local — the “DHCP failed” address) and 8.8.8.8 (public DNS).

← All tools
05
Networking · from the common ports guide

Port lookup

Search by number or service name. These are the doors you will meet in every scan, log and interview.

A port being open is not automatically a vulnerability — what matters is which service answers, whether it is needed, and whether it is patched. Telnet (23), FTP (21) and SMB (445) exposed to the internet are the classic red flags.

← All tools
06
Web & tools · everyday utilities

Base64 & URL encoder

Encode and decode the two formats you will bump into constantly — in URLs, tokens, headers and CTF challenges.

Copied.

Remember: Base64 is encoding, not encryption — anyone can decode it. It exists to carry binary data safely through text-only channels, never to keep secrets.

CIDR quick reference

The prefixes you will actually meet. Every step right halves the hosts and doubles the subnets.

CIDRSubnet maskTotal addressesUsable hostsTypical use
/8255.0.0.016,777,21616,777,214Huge private ranges (10.0.0.0/8)
/16255.255.0.065,53665,534Large office or campus network
/24255.255.255.0256254Home and small-office LAN
/25255.255.255.128128126Splitting a /24 in two
/26255.255.255.1926462One department or device group
/27255.255.255.2243230Small segment — cameras, printers
/28255.255.255.2401614Tiny segment
/30255.255.255.25242Point-to-point router link
/32255.255.255.25511A single host route

Understand the terrain

Build your toolkit

Real attacks, plain English

Breach News: how the big ones actually happened.

Short, honest breakdowns of the attacks everyone is talking about — what happened, how the attackers got in, and the one lesson worth stealing for your own security. Figures are as reported by the source linked in each story.

CRITICAL · ACTIVE EXPLOITATION28 Oct 2026

PolyShell: the flaw that turned online stores into card skimmers

Hundreds of Adobe Commerce and Magento stores breached in an active attack wave — CISA confirmed exploitation in the wild and added the flaws to its KEV catalog.

HIGH · DATA THEFT27 Oct 2026

Sony breach: 2.58 million internet accounts exposed — but not PlayStation

Sony confirmed 2.58 million So-net and plala records exposed — and passwords for 54,401 email accounts leaked. PlayStation accounts were not affected.

HIGH · EXTORTION23 Oct 2026

PwC extortion claim: 590 GB of learning data, and a five-day countdown

The Everest group claims 590 GB stolen from a vendor hosting PwC employee learning records — with a five-day countdown to release.

HIGH · DATA EXPOSURE22 Oct 2026

SBI dark-web find: 3,897 customer records among 375,000 leaked files

SBI found 3,897 customer records with personal details among 375,000 files on the dark web — and warned the real danger is the phishing wave that follows.

CRITICAL · CVSS 9.221 Oct 2026

PHP2Shell: one request could take over most of the web

Two critical flaws in PHP itself — the language behind WordPress and much of the web — let anyone run code on a web server with a single request, no login needed. Japan took major websites offline rather than risk it.

CRITICAL · CVSS 9.527 Sep 2026

NetScaler zero-days: root at the front door, weeks before the fix

Attackers had root access on Citrix NetScaler gateways — the boxes guarding company networks — weeks before anyone knew the flaws existed. And a patch alone will not throw them out.

HIGH · DATA THEFTMay 2026

Canvas breach: a school platform held to ransom in finals season

One flaw in a free-teacher feature put data tied to a claimed 275 million learners at risk — then the ransom note appeared on hundreds of school login pages.

CRITICAL · DESTRUCTIVE11 Mar 2026

Stryker: the company wiped by its own device manager

No malware. No ransom demand. Attackers logged in as admins and used the company’s own management tool to factory-reset its device fleet across 79 countries.

The Hack With K method

Security education should make you more capable, not more confused.

01

Start with the “why”

A command is easier to remember when you understand the system behind it.

02

Show the full chain

Connect networking, operating systems and web behavior instead of teaching isolated facts.

03

Practice ethically

Use permission-based labs, document your work and learn to recommend fixes.
